newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian banks seen raising base lending rates.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian banks seen raising base lending rates.

text.p: High interbank rates in Malaysia could lead to another increase in bank base lending rates next month, analysts said on Thursday.
They said it would not be surprising to see bank base lending rates in double-digits.

With the exception of the country's largest bank, Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank), banks are now quoting their base lending rates at between 9.45 and 9.65 percent, after raising rates by an average 30 basis points on the back of a surge in interbank rates in May.
Maybank on Monday said it was lifting its base lending rate -- the benchmark commercial loan rate banks offer their best customers -- to 9.35 percent from 9.10 percent effective July 15.

Under a new formula announced in October 1995, the calculation of bank base lending rates was pegged to an average of the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) over a one-month period. Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, then fixed a ceiling rate for bank base lending rates.
The ceiling in June was fixed at 9.67 percent. The base lending rate is a key rate used as a benchmark for other commercial rates.
"If based on the formula, base lending rates will have to go up," said Mustafa Mohd Nor, chief economist at Arab Malaysian Securities. "They could go above 10 percent."
Analysts expect banks to raise their base lending rates close to the maximum level allowed.
"I don't think banks can fully absorb the cost of funding. They would want to recover back," Mustafa said.

Interbank rates rose sharply last week, triggered by a sudden tightening of liquidity in the banking system as a result of Bank Negara's massive intervention in the foreign exchange market to defend the ringgit from speculative attacks.
Although the actual size of the intervention was not known, dealers have estimated that between $1 billion and $2 billion was drained from the system.
It led to the overnight interbank rate soaring to 50 percent and three-month money rates jumping to over 15.0 percent.
Analysts said with speculative pressure on the ringgit far from over, rates were likely to be kept high for the time being.

"Rates would have to remain high for a while because of the currency. I think the three-month will hover around 10 percent for a while until the currency thing blows over," said Eddie Lee, regional economist at Vickers Ballas.
"If confidence is low in your currency, you have to keep up interest rates," he said.

The ringgit has fallen about 3.2 percent this week as speculators found a fresh target after hitting on the Thai baht and Philippine peso. At 0400 GMT, the ringgit was quoted at 2.5875 to the dollar. Its weakest level this week was 2.5900. Analysts said the high interest rate environment, however, would not last long, adding that bank base lending rates should start easing in August.
Acting Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday that Malaysia does not favour a high interest rate regime in the long-term.
He said the recent rise in interest rates was due to events in the foreign exchange market.
Businessmen have started to express their displeasure over the high interest rates.
"No businessman can be comfortable with that level of interest rates," said Abdul Rashid Hussain, executive chairman of Rashid Hussain Bhd, Malaysia's largest stockbroking group.
"Higher interest rates do damage to the equity market," he said.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
